kzz7yh-d1e109.summary: Richard of Middleton's Prologue to Book I covers all three of its items: the Praeambulum, Article 1 and the Circa litteram. Its core is Article 1, a nine-question treatise on the nature of theology. Theology is necessary because humanity's final end, the beatifying vision and enjoyment of God, is knowable only by revelation. It is a science subalternated to the knowledge of God and the blessed, with the articles of faith as principles. It is one science because everything in it is referred to God, its subject. It is more practical than speculative, with praxis extended to the will's love of God as the supreme good. It is the noblest and most certain science, wisdom itself, with other disciplines as its handmaids. The Sentences are an ordered collection of questions in service of Scripture, whose argumentative mode they imitate imperfectly. Around this, the Praeambulum reads Lombard's own prologue as a rhetorical exordium making the reader attentive, docile and benevolent. The Circa litteram glosses its wording, defending commentary as making explicit what Scripture implicitly contains and explaining how truth can be hated only per accidens.
claims: Theology is necessary because the final end is knowable only by revelation.
Theology is a subalternate, unified, chiefly practical science whose subject is God.
Theology is the noblest science and true wisdom.
The Sentences are an ordered compilation of questions serving theology.
Exposition makes explicit what Scripture implicitly contains rather than adding to it.

kzz7yh-d1e2449.summary: Book I, distinction 37 covers all five items: the Praeambulum, Articles 1–3 and the Circa litteram. It treats God's presence in things and then the location and motion of angels. The Praeambulum divides Lombard's text on God's existence in things (common presence, indwelling by grace, exclusion of mutable presence) and announces the three articles. Article 1 holds that God is in all things by essence, presence and power, equally in the common mode but unequally by grace, supremely in Christ's humanity. Ubiquity per se and primo is proper to God through his immensity, which exceeds the world without implying any extramundane space. Article 2 develops a theory of angelic location against the operation-only view condemned at Paris. An angel is in place definitively by its simultas with place. Its positive but finite spiritual magnitude lets it be whole in each part of a space that has a maximum but no minimum, and it can be neither multilocated nor co-located with another angel by created power. Article 3 holds that angels move themselves through their act-potency composition and traverse the medium successively, since finite power and divisible space suffice for succession. Their motion has a first change as departure but none as acquisition. The Circa litteram adds that angelic motion is measured by time broadly taken and angelic being by the aevum.
claims: God is in all things by essence, presence and power; unequally present by grace.
Ubiquity per se and primo is proper to God.
Angels are located definitively by simultas, not by operation alone.
Angels cannot be multilocated or co-located by created power.
Angelic local motion traverses the medium successively.

kzz7yh-d1e3298.summary: Book II, distinction 44 covers all five items: the Praeambulum, Articles 1–3 and the Circa litteram. It moves from the power of sinning to the theology of authority and obedience, closing Book II. The Praeambulum divides Lombard's treatment of the power to sin and of the devil's power, and announces three topics: the power of sinning, the power of ruling and the necessity of obedience. Article 1 treats the power to sin as the will plus a defectibility rooted in creation from nothing: a power in essence, an impotence as defectible. God causes the positive being of the sinful act, while its deformity has only a deficient cause. Article 2 holds that all ruling power is from God in its essence but only permissively in unjust acquisition and abuse. It distinguishes dominion as use, as directive command and as coercion; coercion arises only from the Fall and ceases in glory. Article 3 bounds obedience by the limits of authority. Kings may impose new taxes on free subjects only for the common good in necessity, and religious profession does not cancel natural and divine-law duties to parents. The Circa litteram ties obedience to plenary jurisdiction (the Pope, and above all God).
claims: The power to sin is a defectible power; God causes the act's being but not its deformity.
All ruling power is from God in essence; unjust acquisition and abuse are only permitted.
Coercive dominion is a consequence of the Fall.
Obedience is owed only within the limits of legitimate authority.
New taxation of free subjects requires the common good and necessity.
